JUSTICE S.B. SHERR:—

1:     INTRODUCTION

[
1
]

The Children’s Aid Society of Toronto (“the
society”) has brought a summary judgment motion pursuant to
rule 16
of the
Family
Law Rules
, O. Reg. 114/99, as amended (“the rules”), requesting the
following orders:

(a)

that Brittney P. (born on 5
January 2007) be made a Crown ward, without access, for the purpose of
adoption;

(b)

that Irene Faith Mercedes P.
(born on 16 January 2001) and Christina Ellen Selena P. (born on 10 August
2003) be found to be children in need of protection pursuant to
subclauses
37(2)
(
b
)(i) and (ii) of the
Child and Family Services Act
,
R.S.O. 1990, c. C-11, as amended (the Act); that they be placed in the care
and custody of their paternal grandparents, Mrs. Rose H. and Mr. Ron H. (“the
paternal grandparents”), subject to society supervision for six months; that
access to their mother, the respondent Ms. Judy P. (“the mother”), be
supervised and at the discretion of the society and that access to their
father, the respondent Mr. Kurt H. (“the father”), be supervised by the
paternal grandparents, unless otherwise approved by the society and

(c)

that Ms. Judy P. be restrained
and prohibited from making direct or indirect contact with the paternal
grandparents pursuant to
subsection 80(1)
of the
Act
.

[
2
]

The mother opposes the society’s motion.
She has brought her own motion seeking to reinstate access to Brittney P.,
which has been suspended since 26 September 2008, pursuant to a court order.

[
3
]

The father supports the society’s motion with
respect to Irene Faith Mercedes P. and Christina Ellen Selena P.  He takes no
position with respect to Brittney P.

[
4
]

Counsel for Irene Faith Mercedes P. and
Christina Ellen Selena P., from the Office of the Children’s Lawyer, supports
the society’s motion for summary judgment with respect to her clients.

[
5
]

The issue for me to determine is whether
there is a triable issue with respect to one or more of the orders that the
society seeks.  If I find that there is a triable issue with respect to the
order sought for Brittney P., I must then decide whether to reinstate the
mother’s access to her.

2:     PRIOR COURT PROCEEDINGS

[
6
]

Brittney P. was born at Scarborough General
Hospital, but was soon moved to the Hospital for Sick Children in Toronto
because of severe medical problems.  She had to remain hospitalized for six
months after her birth with oesophageal atresia, which means that her
oesophagus was not fully formed.  She required significant care, including
G-tube feeding.  The society commenced its original protection application on 6
June 2007, seeking an order placing Brittney P. with her parents, subject to
society supervision.  On 14 June 2007, Justice Robert J. Spence made a
temporary order, without prejudice, on these terms.  On 27 June 2007, the
society apprehended Brittney P., who was still hospitalized.  On 3 July 2007,
Justice Harvey P. Brownstone made a temporary order, without prejudice, placing
Brittney P. in society care, with access to the parents in the society’s
discretion, in accordance with her medical needs.

[
7
]

On 30 October 2007, Justice Spence noted the
parents in default.  They had failed to file an answer and plan of care,
despite being granted two prior filing extensions.  He found Brittney P. to be
a child in need of protection pursuant to
clause 37(2)
(
a
),
subclause
37(2)
(
b
)(i) and clause 37(2)(
e
) of the
Act
.  He made Brittney P.
a society ward for six months and ordered that the parents’ access be
supervised and in accordance with her medical needs.  She has remained in
society care since that time.

[
8
]

The society apprehended Irene Faith Mercedes
P. and Christina Ellen Selena P. from the parents’ care on 28 December 2007.
On 2 January 2008, Justice Spence made a temporary order placing them in
society care.  He varied this order on 10 January 2008, placing these children
with the paternal grandparents, subject to society supervision, and granting
the parents supervised access.  Irene Faith Mercedes P. and Christina Ellen
Selena P. have lived with the paternal grandparents since then.

[
9
]

On 19 August 2008, Justice Spence, in
response to the mother’s poor attendance record at access visits, ordered that
the mother’s access to Brittney P. should be suspended pending further court
order, if the mother either missed two consecutive visits or was more than ten minutes
late to two consecutive visits.  The society suspended the mother’s access
after she missed her visit of 26 September 2008 and she has not seen Brittney
P. since then.

[
10
]

The parents have never requested a temporary
care and custody motion with respect to any of the children.  Aside from the
mother’s current request to reinstate access to Brittney P., they have also not
brought any motion to increase access to any of the children.

[
11
]

The parents had not filed responding
material to this motion by the original hearing date of 24 October 2008.  The
mother sought an adjournment (which was contested), indicating that she wanted
a new lawyer.  I granted this adjournment, given the serious nature of the
society’s motion and to give the mother every opportunity to put her best foot
forward.

[
12
]

The mother retained new counsel and filed a
lengthy affidavit. The father did not file any material.

3:     THE LAW ON SUMMARY JUDGMENT

[
13
]

Rule 16 of the rules permits a party to make
a motion for summary judgment.  The following provisions in rule 16 are
relevant to this case:

16.   When available.—
(1)   After the respondent has served an answer or
after the time for serving an answer has expired, a party may make a motion
for summary judgment for a final order without a trial on all or part of any
claim made or any defence presented in the case.

.  .  .

(4)
Evidence
required.—
The party making the motion shall serve an
affidavit or other evidence that sets out specific facts showing that there
is no genuine issue requiring a trial.

(4.1)
Evidence of
responding party.—
In response to the affidavit or other
evidence served by the party making the motion, the party responding to the
motion may not rest on mere allegations or denials but shall set out, in an
affidavit or other evidence, specific facts showing that there is a genuine
issue for trial.

(5)
Evidence not from
personal knowledge.—
If a party’s evidence is not from a
person who has personal knowledge of the facts in dispute, the court may draw
conclusions unfavourable to the party.

(6)
No issue for
trial.—
If there is no genuine issue requiring a trial
of a claim or defence, the court shall make a final order accordingly.

.  .  .

[
14
]

On a motion for summary judgment, the court
is required to take a hard look at the merits of the case to determine whether
there is a genuine issue for trial.  The onus is on the society to show that
there is no genuine issue for trial.  See
Children’s
Aid Society of Hamilton v. M.N.
and H.S.N.
,
2007 CanLII 13503
, 156
A.C.W.S. (3d) 1043, [2007] O.J. No. 1526, 2007 Cars­well­Ont 2453 (Ont. Fam.
Ct.).

[
15
]

Summary judgment should proceed with
caution.  It is not, however, limited to or granted only in the clearest of
cases.  The court must ensure the best interests of the child are adequately
addressed on the available evidence.  If the evidence does not raise a triable
issue as to where the best interests lie, those best interests themselves call
for a resolution without the delay associated with the trial and the resulting
prolongation of the state of uncertainty about the child’s future.  See
Jewish
Family and Child Service of Toronto v. R.A. and J.G.

(2001), 102 A.C.W.S.
(3d) 554, 20 L.W.C.D. 251, [2001] O.J. No. 47
, 2001 Cars­well­Ont 73 (Ont.
S.C.),
per
Justice G. Dennis Lane; affirming
Jewish
Family and Child Service of Toronto v. R.A. and J.G.
,
2000 CanLII
22546
, [2000] O.J. No. 6045, 2000 Cars­well­Ont 5169 (Ont. C.J.),
per

Justice Geraldine F. Waldman.

[
16
]

The court’s role on a summary judgment
motion is narrowly limited to assessing the threshold issue of whether a
genuine issue exists as to material requiring a trial.  Because summary
judgment is now explicitly contemplated by
rule 16
, this may “broaden the use
of the procedure as it will no longer be characterized as an extraordinary
remedy.  Nevertheless, the considerations of due process, statutory
requirements and the best interest, protection and well-being of the children
will determine ultimately the appropriateness of summary judgment.”  See
Children’s
Aid Society of Waterloo Region v. Taryn S. and Eric P.
, (
1999 CanLII 14252
, 100 A.C.W.S. (3d) 820, 14
O.F.L.R. 90, [1999] O.J. No. 5561, 1999 Cars­well­Ont 4859 (Ont. C.J.),
per

Justice Paddy A. Hardman.

[
17
]

A party answering a motion for summary
judgment cannot just rest on bald denials; they must put their best foot
forward, showing that there is a genuine issue for trial.  See
Children’s
Aid Society of Toronto v. Kathleen T. and Charles W.
,
2000 CanLII
20578
, 101 A.C.W.S. (3d) 944, [2000] O.J. No. 4736, 2000 Cars­well­Ont 4827
(Ont. C.J.),
per
Justice Penny J. Jones.

[
18
]

The court is not to assess credibility, draw
inferences from conflicting affidavits or weigh the evidence at a summary
judgment motion.  This is reserved for the trier of fact.  See
Children’s
Aid Society of Nipissing v. Marielle M.
,
2000 CanLII 22922
, 98 A.C.W.S.
(3d) 134, [2000] O.J. No. 2541, 2000 Cars­well­Ont 2372 (Ont. S.C.),
per

Justice George T. Valin; affirming
Children’s
Aid Society of Nipissing v. Marielle M.
,
1999
CanLII 15207
, 109 A.C.W.S. (3d) 747, [1999] O.J. No. 5720, 1999 Cars­well­Ont
4938 (Ont. C.J.),
per
Justice Louisette
Duchesneau-McLachlan; and
Children’s
Aid Society of Hamilton v. M.N.
and H.S.N.
,
supra
.

[
19
]

Not every disagreement between the parties
means that a trial is required.  Only a disagreement about a fact that a party
is required to prove constitutes disagreement about a material fact.  See
Children’s
Aid Society of Waterloo Region v. Tara Lee H. and David Scott C.
,
2005
ONCJ 194
, 139 A.C.W.S. (3d) 1028, [2005] O.J. No. 2371, 2005 Cars­well­Ont 8104
(Ont. C.J.),
per
Justice Margaret A. McSorley; affirmed at
David
Scott C. v. Children’s Aid Society of Waterloo Region
,
2006 CanLII
4243
, 145 A.C.W.S. (3d) 1070, [2006] O.J. No. 569, 2006 Cars­well­Ont 849 (Ont.
S.C.),
per
Justice Ronald C. Sills.

[
20
]

A child’s need for permanency planning
within a timeframe sensitive to that child’s needs demands that the legal
process not be used as a strategy to “buy” a parent time to develop an ability
to parent.  In child protection proceedings, the genuineness of an issue must
arise from something more than a heartfelt expression of a parent’s desire to
resume care of the child.  There must be an arguable notion discernible from
the parent’s evidence that she faces some better prospects than what existed at
the time of the society’s removal of the child from her care and has developed
some new ability as a parent.  See
Children’s
Aid Society of Toronto v. Robin H. and Michael N.
,
2000 CanLII 3158
,
131 A.C.W.S. (3d) 455, [2000] O.J. No. 5853, 2000 Cars­well­Ont 6170 (Ont.
C.J.),
per
Justice Heather L. Katarynych.

[
21
]

As Justice Alex Pazaratz stated at paragraph [43] of
Children’s
Aid Society of Niagara Region v. S.C. and B.M.
,

2008 CanLII 52309
, [2008] W.D.F.L. 5026, [2008] O.J.
No. 3969, 2008 Cars­well­Ont 5929 (Ont. Fam. Ct.): “no genuine issue for trial
exists where there is no realistic possibility of an outcome other than that as
sought by the applicant.”

4:     PRELIMINARY COMMENTS

[
22
]

The mother filed a lengthy affidavit
disputing many facts.  However, a large portion of her affidavit was devoted to
contesting the facts that led to the finding that Brittney P. was a child in
need of protection.  The time to contest those facts was when the original protection
application was brought.  The mother chose not to do this and the facts presented
by the society were accepted by the court.  She did not appeal this decision.
On a status review application, the court will not go back and review previous
orders and findings of fact but must focus on the long-term interests of the
child.  See
Children's
Aid Society of Ottawa v. M.S.
et al.
,
2005 CanLII 42251
, 143 A.C.W.S.
(3d) 699, [2006] W.D.F.L. 184, [2005] O.J. No. 4885, 2005 Cars­well­Ont 6649
(Ont. Fam. Ct.).  Further, much of the mother’s affidavit consisted of bald
denials of material facts.  Where she had the opportunity of providing corroborating
evidence to dispute a material fact, such as by providing medical records, or
evidence from her new partner, she generally failed to do so.  Although there
are several facts that are in dispute, their determination would not change the
outcome of this case.

[
23
]

I have decided that there is no triable
issue with respect to the following orders sought by the society:

(a)

that Brittney P. should be made
a Crown ward without access for the purpose of adoption;

(b)

that Irene Faith Mercedes P. and
Christina Ellen Selena P. are children in need of protection under the Act and
it is in their best interests that they be placed in the care and custody of
the paternal grandparents, for six months, subject to society supervision;
and

(c)

that the mother’s access to
Irene Faith Mercedes P. and Christina Ellen Selena P. needs to remain fully
supervised, subject to the discretion of the society, and that the father’s
access should be supervised by the paternal grandparents, unless otherwise
approved by the society.

[
24
]

I have decided that there is a triable issue
with respect to the society’s request for the restraining order.

[
25
]

I will set out the evidence and analysis
upon which I rely below.

5:     BRITTNEY P.

5.1:     Brittney P. as a Child
in Need of Protection

[
26
]

The following material facts were not
contested when Justice Spence, on 30 October 2007, made the finding that
Brittney P. was a child in need of protection:

(a)

The society had several file
openings with this family from 2001 to 2006.  These concerned issues such as
domestic violence between the parents in front of Irene Faith Mercedes P. and
Christina Ellen Selena P., the state of their living conditions and improper
supervision of these children.  None of the file openings, prior to 2006
resulted in a court application.

(b)

In 2006, the mother’s
obstetrician and diabetes nurse specialist both reported to the society
concerns about the mother’s lack of pre-natal care for Brittney P.; that her
pregnancy was high risk due to her serious diabetes and that she was not following
through with proper management of her blood sugar levels, or attending recommended
appointments, placing the foetus at risk.  She only saw the obstetrician once
at 26 weeks.  These concerns were reiterated on 9 January 2007 by a second
obstetrician whom the mother began seeing towards the end of her pregnancy.

(c)

The mother’s first obstetrician
reported to the society that Brittney P.’s condition is highly associated
with uncontrolled diabetes during pregnancy.  Justice Spence’s finding under

clause 37(2)
(
a
) of the
Act
could only have been based on the finding
that the mother’s failure to obtain appropriate medical care was a likely
contributor to Brittney P.’s medical condition.  This clause reads as
follows:

(2)
Child in need of
protection.—
A child is in need of protection where,

(a)

the child has suffered physical harm,
inflicted by the person having charge of the child or caused by or resulting
from that person’s,

(i)

failure to adequately care for, provide
for, supervise or protect the child, or

(ii)

pattern of neglect in caring for,
providing for, supervising or protecting the child;

(d)

Brittney P.’s primary physician

A breach of a restraining order can have
severe repercussions, including imprisonment, and the court must be careful
